title: Eric Schmidt and Sergey Brin Clash Over $100 Million California Tax Fight Strategy
excerpt: The former Google CEO is reportedly frustrated with how their shared anti-tax coalition has deployed funds, as California Democrats endorse a billionaire wealth tax.
body:
• Eric Schmidt has grown frustrated with Sergey Brin's leadership of an anti-tax coalition that has spent over $100 million opposing California's Proposition 40 billionaire wealth tax
  • The rift centers on coalition funds being diverted to fight other ballot measures, including Proposition 45 on environmental policy, instead of focusing solely on defeating the wealth tax
  • California Democrats endorsed Proposition 40 at their convention, narrowly clearing the 61.7% threshold despite the billionaire-backed opposition effort
  • Brin has personally contributed over $100 million to the political organisation Building a Better California, while Schmidt has put in over $3 million

The Political Rift

Eric Schmidt and Sergey Brin helped build Google into one of the world's most valuable technology companies. Now, the former CEO and the co-founder find themselves on the same side of a California political fight—but increasingly at odds over how to wage it.

The New York Post reported Sunday that Schmidt has grown frustrated with the anti-tax coalition led in large part by Brin after the group failed to prevent California Democrats from endorsing Proposition 40, a ballot measure that would impose a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California residents whose wealth exceeds $1 billion. The proposition is backed by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West and championed by Democratic Party leaders Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna.

"His only current involvement in politics is his contributions to defeating the billionaires tax."

— Advisor to Eric Schmidt, speaking to Fortune

Where the Money Went

Both Schmidt and Brin have poured millions into Building a Better California, the political organisation established to oppose Proposition 40. Brin has supplied the majority of the funding, contributing over $100 million. Schmidt has contributed over $3 million. Other major donors include venture capitalist John Doerr ($7.5 million), Ripple executive chair Chris Larsen ($10 million), and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison ($7 million).

According to an advisor to Schmidt, the former Google CEO's frustration stems not from the Democratic endorsement outcome itself, but from the coalition's decision to deploy funds against other ballot measures—including Proposition 45, an environmental policy measure—rather than concentrating solely on defeating the wealth tax.

The Ballot Battle

The coalition's strategic setback extends beyond Proposition 40. Propositions 41 and 42, two counter-measures backed by Schmidt and Brin through Building a Better California, were also opposed by the Democratic Party. Proposition 41 would require state audits of programmes funded by new special taxes, while Proposition 42 would outlaw retroactive taxation—directly countering Proposition 40. The party narrowly passed the endorsement threshold at 61.7%.

California's Legislative Analyst's Office estimates the wealth tax would affect a few hundred people and could produce tens of billions of dollars in revenue. Schmidt, whose Bloomberg-estimated wealth stands at $58.1 billion, would be directly affected.

Tech Billionaires Push Back

The Schmidt-Brin disagreement is just one thread in a broader tech-industry backlash against the proposed tax. Mark Cuban recently engaged in a public seven-part debate on X with Congressman Ro Khanna over the measure's implications. Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey has also clashed with Khanna online, calling the proposal "extraordinarily frustrating politician-speak that nobody in the industry is dumb enough to fall for."

All three measures—Proposition 40 and the two counter-proposals—still go before voters in November, meaning the political fight is far from over regardless of party endorsements.

A Complicated Legacy

The tension between Schmidt and Brin adds a personal dimension to an already high-stakes political battle. Schmidt served as Google's CEO from 2001 to 2011 before becoming executive chairman. Their relationship has had friction points before—Schmidt reportedly lost influence after siding against Brin and Larry Page on Google's decision to withdraw censored searches from China in 2010. This latest disagreement, however, is playing out in the open arena of California politics rather than behind corporate boardroom doors.
